title: Leaving Anandpur
hookLine: after a long siege and broken promises of safe passage, the family is scattered crossing the flooded Sarsa river
last: WONDERFUL THE GURU, WONDERFUL THE DISCIPLE.

lines: THE HILL RAJAS AND THE MUGHALS.
cards: Anandpur, surrounded. The birth of the Khalsa had worried the powerful. The hill rajas around Anandpur saw a growing force on their doorstep that ignored caste and owed them nothing.
Over the next few years they fought the Guru, and then they called on the Mughal governors for help. These days of the story are remembered each December, in homes and gurdwaras.
They are hard, so this goes a piece at a time. Today, the siege, the promise, and a flooded river on a winter night.

teach.b: The siege of Anandpur went on for months. Nothing could get in. Food ran out; tradition says the defenders ate leaves and bark.

teach.h: A PROMISE OF SAFE PASSAGE, BROKEN.
teach.b: Then the besiegers sent a promise: leave Anandpur, and you'll have safe passage. Tradition says the promise came with sacred oaths, sworn on the holy books of the besiegers' own faiths, and the Guru was deeply doubtful.
But his people were starving, and at last, in December, on a bitter night, the whole household and the remaining Sikhs came out and headed south. The promise was broken almost at once.
The besieging army attacked the column as it moved. At the Sarsa river, swollen with winter rain, they had to cross in the dark, under attack. Many drowned.
Tradition says precious manuscripts, the Guru's writings among them, were swept away.
And on that riverbank, the family was scattered. The Guru, with his two elder sons and a small band of Sikhs, went one way.
His mother, Mata Gujri, with the two youngest boys, aged about nine and six, was separated and went another, with a family servant. The Guru's wives were led to safety toward Delhi.
None of them knew if they would see the others again.
Today's line holds onto one thing: scattered is not lost. Each part of the family carried the same faith into the dark.
Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit they kept: chardi kala, rising spirits, courage that keeps climbing when everything else is falling.

how: Each December, Sikhs remember the evacuation of Anandpur and the separation of the Guru's family, with gatherings, recitation and langar at gurdwaras along the route, including Gurdwara Parivar Vichhora on the Sarsa.

p: a promise broken almost at once

games.q: you're the Guru. your people are starving, and the besiegers swear on their holy books to give you safe passage. what do you do?
o: refuse and hold out to the end.
leave, though you doubt the promise.
games.why: tradition says the Guru doubted the oaths but, for his starving people, left. the promise was broken almost at once.

practice: Think of someone you love who is far away right now, in another city, another country, or out of reach in some other way, and picture where they might be at this moment.
Hold them there, safely, in your mind, as if you were keeping a light on for them. If you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Leaving Anandpur. After a long siege and a broken promise of safe passage, the Guru's family was scattered crossing the flooded Sarsa river.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: rising spirits, the Sikh ideal of courage that keeps climbing.

carryVoice: Your line: scattered, not lost. A siege, a broken promise, a river in the dark. Until tomorrow.
